problem: Visual encoders for robot navigation are either ImageNet-pretrained (focus on salient objects, not navigation-relevant regions) or trained end-to-end from scratch (expensive). Contrastive SSL is hard to apply because negative samples are ill-defined in action space.
motivation: Humans attend only to the regions that affect their trajectory. A navigation-specific self-supervised pretext task could give small, efficient CNN encoders that focus on navigation-relevant regions with little data and training time.
key_idea: Pre-train a CNN visual encoder without negatives by using VICReg to maximize information between embeddings of past image history, future actions and a future goal image, each produced through small Transformer encoders.
insight: Actions alone are sparse and give poor long-horizon results (5s MSE 0.499), while goal images add richer but redundant cues (0.392). Combining both helps, and using the goal only as a supervision target (GoalOut, 0.383) beats feeding it into the Transformer (GoalIn, 0.386). Random-crop augmentation avoids collapse on static sequences and lets the dataset grow from 11k to 26k samples. Activation maps show VANP attends to multiple navigation regions (paths, obstacles), whereas end-to-end and ImageNet encoders attend to single salient regions.
method: Image encoder: ResNet-50 without classification head (VANP-50) encodes each frame of a 6-frame history and the goal image; a 4-layer, 4-head TransformerEncoder with a context token aggregates them into Z^i (512-d)
Action encoder: a second TransformerEncoder with a context token embeds 20 future actions (2-d velocities, 4 Hz, 5 s) into Z^a
Goal embedding: the same CNN encodes the future goal image I_{t+tau_F} into Z^g, used only as a supervision target (GoalOut)
Objective: L = lambda*VICReg(Z^i,Z^g) + (1-lambda)*VICReg(Z^i,Z^a), with variance/covariance regularizers, so no negatives are needed; 3-layer MLP projection heads output 1024-d
Augmentation: VICReg-style augmentations, notably random crop to add inter-frame variation and avoid collapse on static sequences
Downstream: an MLP on the Transformer context token predicts 3s and 5s trajectories from image history and polar local goal; the encoder is either frozen or fine-tuned

setting.backbone: ResNet-50 (+ 4-layer Transformer encoders) pretrained with VANP self-supervision; the downstream MLP policy is trained on top
setting.model_size: ResNet-50 (~25M) + small Transformers; VANP-18 variant used on robot
setting.training_data: About 11,000 curated samples from SCAND (8.7 h) and MuSoHu (~20 h) real-world egocentric navigation data (26,042 with augmentation); 8,000 unseen samples for evaluation; about 0.08% of ImageNet size
setting.observation: Monocular egocentric RGB, 6-frame history at 98x126, plus polar local goal
setting.action_space: Continuous linear and angular velocity trajectories (20 steps at 4 Hz; predicts 3s and 5s horizons)
setting.simulator: none (offline real-world datasets); real-world Jackal demo

numbers.eval_set_note: 8,000 unseen samples from SCAND and MuSoHu; metric is MSE of predicted trajectory vs ground truth

numbers_note: Only offline trajectory-prediction MSE is reported; there are no standard navigation benchmark numbers (no SR/SPL). The real-robot experiment is qualitative.
results: VANP is comparable to end-to-end models trained from scratch (best fine-tuned 0.103/0.272 vs 0.116/0.307 3s/5s) with half the training time. It is comparable to ImageNet weights with only 0.08% of the data. Frozen multi-frame VANP (0.133/0.342) clearly beats frozen ImageNet (0.169/0.435), but frozen single-frame ImageNet is best at 3s (0.129).
limitations: Works best when the goal image is visible from the current frame, and collapses on sequences with no inter-frame change; scaling to large noisy datasets is uncertain
Small curated dataset (~11k samples), offline MSE evaluation only, and no standard nav benchmarks
Real-robot demo is only a proof of concept: it fails on small obstacles and only works in uncluttered environments
